matchup_findings.statement: UCLA's defense out-rates the opposing offense on a down-to-down basis (-2.46 for Michigan's offense).

UCLA owns the stronger opponent-adjusted scoring matchup: Michigan offense vs UCLA defense -2.61, UCLA offense vs Michigan defense -0.20 (points per game, opponent-adjusted: UCLA offense #26 of 138, Michigan defense #24 of 138).
UCLA's defense generates sacks and negative plays against an offense that allows them (-1.38 for Michigan's offense).
UCLA holds the early-down edge: its offense stays ahead of the chains on 1st and 2nd down against this defense (-0.78) more than Michigan does (-2.67).

UCLA owns the stronger opponent-adjusted explosive-play matchup: Michigan offense vs UCLA defense -1.61, UCLA offense vs Michigan defense -0.21 (explosive-play rate, opponent-adjusted: UCLA offense #16 of 138, Michigan defense #8 of 138).

UCLA owns the stronger opponent-adjusted sustained-efficiency matchup: Michigan offense vs UCLA defense -2.46, UCLA offense vs Michigan defense -0.64 (success rate, opponent-adjusted: UCLA offense #36 of 138, Michigan defense #15 of 138).
Both offenses and both defenses point to fewer snaps than an average FBS game (possession environment -1.29).
Each offense meets a defense it is held by on opponent-adjusted points (Michigan -2.61, UCLA -0.20).
UCLA's sustained-efficiency edge is real but not decisive (1.82, below the 2.0 strong threshold): enough for the trailing side to stay in range.
UCLA's offense has swung widely from game to game relative to its opponents (game-to-game residual variation in the 88th percentile of FBS).
2 independent volatility indicators are present: this matchup has wide outcomes.
Michigan's offense has given the ball away at a high rate (+1.90 SD). Regression-prone: reported as volatility, never as a cause on its own.
Michigan's leading passer in its last game (Tommy Carr) is not its season leader (Bryce Underwood): season passing numbers may not describe the quarterback who plays.
